source: Coulthart (2015) Improving the Analysis of Foreign Affairs: Evaluating Structured Analytic Techniques (Pitt dissertation) - abstract
finding: Systematic review of a random sample of more than 2,000 studies found moderate to strong support for three SATs: ACH, brainstorming, devil's advocacy. Three main findings: face-to-face collaboration lowers creativity; weighing evidence matters more than seeking disconfirming evidence; conflict tends to improve analysis quality. A small experiment confirmed the first two.
numbers: Sample >2,000 studies (random sample of a larger pool); 12 core SATs evaluated; experiment N=21 graduate intelligence-studies students; also survey of 80 analysts, 15 follow-up interviews, 5 expert interviews.
quote: Questions about the effectiveness of the techniques were answered in part by employing a systematic review
limits: Only the abstract page was readable (the PDF was behind a bot wall). Review method and per-technique effect sizes could not be checked. Studies are mostly non-intelligence (group decision, creativity, lab) work transferred to analysis. Vote-count style synthesis, not a pooled effect size.
agent_relevance: Supports three operator ideas (hypothesis comparison, idea generation, assigned dissent) but the evidence is indirect. Treat as a prior, not proof.

source: Coulthart (2015) dissertation abstract - survey part
finding: Survey of 80 analysts at one US IC agency: 1 in 3 never used SATs. Use was linked to analytic training and perceived value, not to time pressure.
numbers: Training: p=0.001, Cramer's V=0.41. Perceived value: p=.049, V=0.23. Time pressure: p=0.74 (no link). N=80 survey, 15 follow-up interviews.
limits: One agency, self-report. A later paper summarises the same survey as 21% using SATs more than rarely.
agent_relevance: Adoption is driven by trust in value, so a scaffold must show its own measured payoff (matches G7).

source: Coulthart (2017) An Evidence-Based Evaluation of 12 Core Structured Analytic Techniques, Int. J. Intelligence and CounterIntelligence 30(2)
finding: Journal version of the review, as described by a later paper that I did read (Martin 2025): of the 12 SATs in the US Government Tradecraft Primer, only six had any empirical evaluation: Devil's Advocacy, ACH, Brainstorming, Alternative Futures Analysis, Red Teaming, Team A/Team B. The share of studies supporting each ranged from 0 to 100%. Only the first three had evidence credibility above low.
numbers: 6 of 12 SATs with any empirical test; support proportion 0 to 100% by technique; 3 of 6 above low credibility.
limits: Not opened (publisher blocked). Facts are second-hand from Martin 2025 footnotes 7-8. Credibility grades are the reviewer's own.
agent_relevance: Six of twelve popular techniques have no test at all: a reason not to import SAT names into the schema on authority.

source: Martin (2025) The Relationship Between Structured Analytic Techniques and Intelligence Analysis Quality: Evidence from Content Analysis (PsyArXiv preprint)
finding: Content analysis of 138 reports from the IARPA CREATE SWARM challenges (2018, 2020). Quality-of-reasoning (QoR) score and accuracy correlated only weakly. Standardizing Probability Ranges and Timeline predicted QoR; no technique reliably predicted accuracy.
numbers: N=138 reports (accuracy scorable for about 80). QoR vs accuracy: partial r(77)=.25, p=.028; zero-order r(78)=.30. Max single-code |r| with QoR=.28 (Timeline, Standardizing Probability Ranges). Accuracy: no model beat null; best was Timeline, BF10 moderate; post-hoc power analysis needed N=126.
limits: Observational, not randomised; reports chose their own techniques; only 2 of the 12 Primer SATs (ACH, Key Assumptions Check) were used more than once; low power for accuracy; teams large, many were public not professional.
agent_relevance: Adherence to process norms (QoR) is cheap to improve, accuracy is not shown to follow. Do not score the scaffold on process-looking output.

source: Martin (2025) - number of techniques per report
finding: Using more distinct techniques in a report went with better process quality but not clearly with accuracy.
numbers: Unique codes vs QoR: b=.16, t=5.77, p<.001, R2=.19 after controlling team type, zero-order r(135)=.46. Unique codes vs accuracy: b=.07, p=.15, R2=.03, r(78)=.23.
limits: Correlational; longer or more careful reports may use more techniques anyway.
agent_relevance: More steps look more rigorous but may not add accuracy. Supports G7 (schema must pay for itself).

source: Martin (2025) - context on SAT use
finding: Cites an IC review where only 22 of 63 unclassified reports (about 35%) used SATs, and agencies did not track whether SATs help.
numbers: 22/63 reports (about 35%); survey: 21% of 80 analysts use SATs more than rarely.
limits: Second-hand citation of Artner, Girven and Bruce (RAND 2017); the original RAND report was blocked (HTTP 403).
agent_relevance: Real-world use is thin, so the evidence base is mostly lab studies.

source: Wilcox & Mandel (2023, Intelligence and National Security) Critical review of the Analysis of Competing Hypotheses technique: Lessons for the intelligence community
finding: Searched 244 entries; found 7 papers describing 6 distinct experiments with an ACH group and a no-SAT control. Conclusion: ACH as a whole has little to no overall benefit on judgment quality and may harm it, though some parts may help. Authors advise against mandating ACH.
numbers: 244 records screened; 7 papers; 6 experiments. No pooled effect size because outcomes differed. Table 3: accuracy (mean absolute error) shows no difference in studies 2, 4, 5; confirmation-bias reduction positive only in study 1 for novices, null in 1 (experienced), 6, 7; diagnosticity better in 2/3, worse in 4 and 5.
limits: Narrow inclusion (needs a no-SAT control) so it drops studies that compared SATs with each other. Many studies small. Authors say the ACH steps are unclear and its scoring breaks Bayesian norms.
agent_relevance: The most direct negative evidence for the ACH operator. Keep hypothesis comparison but compute scores in code with Bayes, not with ACH inconsistency counting.

source: Lehner, Adelman, Cheikes & Brown (2008) Confirmation bias in complex analyses - via Wilcox & Mandel 2023 table 2
finding: USS Iowa task, four rounds of evidence. ACH did not reduce confirmation bias among experienced analysts; analysts using ACH had less confirmation bias than people with no analytic experience.
numbers: Very small sample: ACH condition had 5 experienced analysts, non-SAT condition 7. Confirmation bias measured as correlation of earlier confidence with later evidence ratings.
limits: Read only through the review table, not the original. Rating scale was changed to -2..+2 and participants were not told how to aggregate.
agent_relevance: Tiny N; do not lean on it. Suggests expertise, not the matrix, drove bias reduction.

source: Mandel, Karvetski & Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails? Judgment and Decision Making 13(6)
finding: Randomised test of ACH with 50 UK intelligence analysts. ACH did not improve probability accuracy or coherence; it was non-significantly worse. ACH did make analysts rate cue usefulness much more accurately. Statistical recalibration plus averaging cut error sharply.
numbers: N=50, about 25 per arm. Mean absolute error: control .21, ACH .26 (p=.14, d=0.45 favouring control). Usefulness tracks probability gain r=.68 ACH vs r=.17 control (d=1.59, p<.001). Unitarity sum control 1.54, ACH 1.77. Coherentising cut error .23 to .15 (35%); averaging all 50 gave .09 (61% cut).
quote: ACH did not improve probability accuracy or coherence
limits: One neat task (4 tribes, 12 cues, naive-Bayes truth that assumes independence), junior analysts (mean 14 months experience), underpowered. Controls could use any method.
agent_relevance: Strongest numbers in the field: code-side normalising and averaging beat the technique. Matches G5 (code normalises) and G4.

source: Dhami, Belton & Mandel (2019) The Analysis of Competing Hypotheses in intelligence analysis, Applied Cognitive Psychology - via Wilcox & Mandel 2023
finding: Same data as Mandel 2018, analysed for process. Most ACH-group analysts deviated from at least one ACH step (for example adding up consistent evidence, which ACH says to ignore). Most control analysts built an ACH-style matrix anyway. ACH group listed all cues correctly more often but used base rates less.
numbers: N=50 (same data). No exact counts retrieved.
limits: Secondary reading through the review; original paywalled. A control group that already builds matrices weakens any contrast.
agent_relevance: People fail to follow multi-step protocols; programmatic enforcement of steps is safer than instructions.

source: Karvetski, Mandel & Irwin (2020) Improving probability judgment in intelligence analysis - via Wilcox & Mandel 2023
finding: Online panel study with mushroom hypotheses. No accuracy difference between ACH and Bayesian-style elicitation when unaggregated; with aggregation ACH was less accurate than the Bayesian elicitation at most group sizes. Judgments were less coherent after ACH than before. People double-counted perfectly correlated cues.
numbers: Sample size not captured in the review text I read; within-subject before/after comparison for ACH.
limits: Lay participants, no training, one task; read second-hand.
agent_relevance: Structured Bayesian updating beats the ACH inconsistency tally. Use the former for the evidence step.

source: Karvetski & Mandel (2020) ACH vs control, graffiti gang task - via Wilcox & Mandel 2023
finding: ACH users were marginally less reliable (gave different probabilities to structurally identical evidence), showed pseudo-diagnosticity, and did not differ in coherence or conservatism.
numbers: N=227 Canadian citizens, one-factor between design.
limits: Lay sample; ACH matrix was pre-populated; pseudo-diagnosticity is the bias ACH is meant to cure.
agent_relevance: A diagnostic-looking matrix can still carry the bias it targets.

source: Whitesmith (2020) ACH and cognitive bias - via Wilcox & Mandel 2023
finding: ACH showed no significant reduction in serial position effects or confirmation bias; confirmation bias also distorted use of ACH's own scoring.
numbers: N=32 King's College students plus 7 UK intelligence community members; 2-hour ACH training; seven information sets.
limits: Small; participants told their belief need not match the ACH score, so aggregation may not have been followed.
agent_relevance: Order effects survive structure. Shuffle evidence order in code.

source: Maegherman et al. (2021) Test of ACH in legal decision-making - via Wilcox & Mandel 2023
finding: ACH did not change guilt judgments or search for information. Little confirmation bias to correct in either group. Only 38% of ACH participants followed instructions and used the matrix.
numbers: N=191 Dutch and Belgian law students; 38% compliance.
limits: Students, one case, brief explanation instead of training.
agent_relevance: Compliance was low even when asked; favours code-enforced steps.

source: Wilcox & Mandel 2023 - rigor assessment
finding: Authors judge the six experiments as varied and often underpowered. They warn small samples both miss real effects and produce effects that will not replicate.
numbers: Sample sizes across experiments run from 12 to 227.
limits: Judgment of rigor is the reviewers' own.
agent_relevance: All 'ACH works' claims in this series should be graded [S] at best.

source: De Dreu & Weingart (2003) Task versus relationship conflict, team performance, and team member satisfaction: a meta-analysis, J Applied Psychology 88(4)
finding: Both relationship conflict and task conflict correlated strongly and negatively with team performance and satisfaction, against the textbook claim that task conflict helps. Harm was larger in complex tasks (decision making, projects) than production tasks. Task conflict hurt less when only weakly tied to relationship conflict.
numbers: Abstract only: exact correlations not read this session.
limits: Abstract only. Studies measure conflict in teams, mostly field surveys.
agent_relevance: Contradicts the simple reading 'conflict improves quality'. Dissent only helps when kept task-focused; relevant to critic and debate roles.

source: De Wit, Greer & Jehn (2012) The paradox of intragroup conflict: a meta-analysis, J Applied Psychology 97(2)
finding: Update after 2003: 116 studies (8,880 groups). Relationship and process conflict stay negative for outcomes. The strong negative task-conflict effect was not replicated. Task conflict related more positively to performance in top management teams, when weakly linked to relationship conflict, and when the outcome was financial performance or decision quality.
numbers: 116 studies, n=8,880 groups.
limits: Abstract only. Moderators tested one by one.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of the De Dreu 2003 pattern. 'Conflict improves quality' holds only under moderators. Use dissent only on a signal (G1) and keep it about the task.

source: Schwenk (1990) Effects of devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry on decision making: A meta-analysis, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 47
finding: Meta-analysis of lab studies of assigned dissent (devil's advocate, dialectical inquiry) against consensus approaches. My recollection: both dissent methods gave better decision quality than consensus, with no clear difference between them.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: UNVERIFIED from memory. Publisher page not accessible. Mostly student lab groups; effect sizes not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Likely the source behind the devil's-advocacy support claim. Verify before use.

source: Mullen, Johnson & Salas (1991) Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: a meta-analytic integration, Basic and Applied Social Psychology 12
finding: Meta-analysis showing interacting brainstorming groups produce fewer ideas than the same number of people working alone (nominal groups). Matches the dissertation finding that face-to-face collaboration lowers creativity.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: UNVERIFIED from memory. Causes usually named: production blocking, evaluation apprehension, free riding.
agent_relevance: Generate candidate hypotheses independently, then merge in code.

source: Chang, Berdini, Mandel & Tetlock (2018) Restructuring structured analytic techniques in intelligence, Intelligence and National Security 33(3)
finding: Cited by Martin 2025 as arguing SATs should be redesigned around judgment-science evidence, and that mandated SATs rest on face validity.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Only a citation seen; publisher blocked.
agent_relevance: Frame: keep only elements with a measured payoff.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum & Mordatch (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate (arXiv 2305.14325)
finding: Several chatGPT instances give answers, read each other's, and revise over rounds. Debate beat single answer, self-reflection and majority vote on math, chess and facts. Reflection hurt factuality on MMLU.
numbers: 3 agents, 2 rounds. Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9. Biographies: 66.0, 68.3, debate 73.8. MMLU: 63.9, 57.7, debate 71.1. Chess validity 29.3, 38.8, 45.2. More agents and rounds helped up to about 4 rounds.
limits: Compared at unequal compute (see Huang 2023 and Smit 2023). Small test samples (about 100 items per cell, wide error bars). One model family (chatGPT).
agent_relevance: The closest AI analogue of devil's advocacy/dialectic. Gains may come from sampling more, not from critique.

source: Liang et al. (2023) Encouraging Divergent Thinking in LLMs through Multi-Agent Debate (arXiv 2305.19118)
finding: Affirmative and negative debaters plus a judge, to fix degeneration of thought where self-reflection locks onto its first answer. Self-reflection showed low disagreement between rounds.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic (200 questions): GPT-3.5 26.0, +CoT 28.0, +self-consistency 29.5, +self-reflect 27.5, +MAD 37.0, GPT-4 51.0. Common MT: MAD with GPT-3.5 beat GPT-4 on automatic and human metrics. Token cost: self-reflect 1.83x CoT; MAD adds 0.63x.
limits: Dataset built by the authors; judge model choice mattered (GPT-3.5 judge 84.4 vs Vicuna-13b 83.2 on MT); tit-for-tat level must be tuned.
agent_relevance: Supports assigned opposition as a fix for anchoring on the first answer, only for tasks where the first instinct is wrong.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A look at multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs (arXiv 2311.17371)
finding: Seven systems on seven datasets with cost and accuracy. No debate protocol beat simple baselines overall. Medprompt was best on average. Multi-Persona improved when its agreement level was tuned.
numbers: Best-run accuracies (MedQA / MMLU / GPQA): Medprompt .65/.74/.27; Society of Mind .64/.73/.27; Single agent .60/.76/.33; Self-consistency .60/.78/.24; Multi-Persona .58/.72/.29.
limits: Table shows best configuration per cell, so winners are picked after the fact; GPT-3.5 mainly.
agent_relevance: Debate is hard to tune and unreliable. Do not make it default.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, ICLR (arXiv 2310.01798)
finding: Without an oracle label, asking the model to review its own answer lowers accuracy. Multi-agent debate gains match self-consistency at equal answer count and lose to it at more samples.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonsenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after one self-correction round; GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after two rounds. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K reaches 95.5 and HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0. GSM8K with 6 responses: debate 83.2 vs self-consistency 85.3.
limits: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2 era. Table extraction for the debate rows was partly garbled; only the 6-response comparison is quoted.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2: revise only from real output. Critique by the same model is not independent evidence.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key? (arXiv 2402.18272)
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt (demonstration) matched the best discussion framework on reasoning tasks. Discussion beat a single agent only when no demonstration was given. The MAD framework with forced disagreement was the weakest, probably because disagreement adds irrelevant information.
numbers: ChatGPT-3.5 table 2: MAD (3 agents) 70.04 and Debate (3 agents) 73.88 and CMD (6 agents) 74.46 in the last column; column labels not fully recoverable, so only the ordering is trusted. Failure types named: Judge Mistake and Wrong Answer Propagation.
limits: Column labels in the extracted table are unclear.
agent_relevance: Counters 'conflict improves quality' for LLMs: forced disagreement can hurt (G1).

source: Khan et al. (2024) Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers (arXiv 2402.06782)
finding: Expert debaters see the text, weaker judges do not. Debate improved judge accuracy over naive reading.
numbers: Non-expert LLM judges 76% with debate vs 48% naive; human judges 88% vs 60%. Optimising debaters raised human-judge accuracy from 88% to 95-98% (appendix text).
limits: Information-asymmetric reading-comprehension task where a ground truth exists in a hidden passage. Not the same as analysis without ground truth.
agent_relevance: Adversarial debate helps when a judge can verify against evidence; supports G3-style checks over opinion.

source: Wynn, Satija & Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate (arXiv 2509.05396)
finding: Debate can lower accuracy over rounds, even when stronger models outnumber weaker ones. Agents flipped correct answers to wrong more often than wrong to right, and flips grew with the number of agreeing peers (conformity).
numbers: Tests on CommonSenseQA, MMLU and GSM8K; counts are in figures, not recorded in the text I read.
limits: Figures not machine-readable in the extract; exact flip rates not captured.
agent_relevance: LLM debaters conform. This is the opposite of what devil's advocacy needs. Link: Conformity subfield.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate (arXiv 2502.08788)
finding: 5 MAD methods x 9 benchmarks x 4 models (36 configurations): MAD usually fails to beat Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency despite more compute. Mixing different models in the debate helps.
numbers: AgentVerse beat CoT in about 15% of cases; ChatEval lost least yet won under 15%; SoM below CoT on all 9 datasets with GPT-4o-mini. MAD better on maths, worse on code. Heter-MAD average gain over CoT-average about +5.8% (SoM variant) and +4.4% (second variant).
limits: Temperature 1, six LLM calls per method; win rate from ANOVA at p<.05 per configuration.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of the early MAD claims with newer models. Diverse models is the lever: use different model families for opposing roles, if any.

source: Chan et al. (2023) ChatEval: Towards Better LLM-based Evaluators through Multi-Agent Debate (arXiv 2308.07201)
finding: A panel of LLM judges with different personas discussing evaluation. Same-persona panels did worse.
numbers: Accuracy vs human labels up 6.2% for ChatGPT and 2.5% for GPT-4 over single-agent; same-role-prompt variant 53.8 accuracy, Kappa 0.25 (ChatGPT). Humans' own average accuracy 71.7%.
limits: Evaluation task, not generation. Gains small for GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Role diversity matters; identical voters add nothing (G4).

source: Zhong et al. (2026) Before the Action: Benchmarking LLMs on Prospective Hypothesis Discovery (arXiv 2607.15766)
finding: HypoEval benchmark, 988 cases in six domains, 15 LLMs. An Agent mode composed 12 structured analytic skills adapted from the SAT handbook (ACH, structured brainstorming, chronology) into a pipeline. Effect was model-dependent: not a uniform gain.
numbers: 988 cases, 15 models. Arena rating change from skills: from about +88 (kimi-k2.5) to about -60 (claude-opus-4.6); Spearman with baseline strength rho=-0.10. Judge vs experts: Kendall tau .90, Spearman .98 on 1,500 pairwise comparisons.
limits: LLM judge ranks outputs (bias risk, though checked against experts); no ground-truth outcomes; failure called candidate compression (rich intermediate analysis squeezed into a narrow final list).
agent_relevance: Most direct 2026 test of SAT-as-scaffold for LLMs. Result: not reliably positive. Keep wide candidate lists to the end (no compression).

source: Chen et al. (2025) HypoSpace: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Set-Valued Hypothesis Generation under Underdetermination (arXiv 2510.15614)
finding: Models keep high validity but lose uniqueness and recovery as the space of valid hypotheses grows (mode collapse). Stratified decoding partly helps.
numbers: Three metrics: Validity, Uniqueness, Recovery. Three domains: causal graphs, 3D voxels, Boolean gene interactions. Exact figures not read (abstract and intro only).
limits: Synthetic domains with enumerable truth.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis generation for ACH-like steps will collapse onto a few modes; use code-side diversity (dedupe, stratified sampling).
